module.title: Unit 3: Me and My Family: Family Members & Possessives
module.objective: Introduce family members, describe personal qualities, use possessive 's and possessive adjectives (this/that/these/those), and give simple compliments in English.

subModules.title: Reading Mission: Meet the Family
subModules.grammarFocus: Possessive 's, Possessive Adjectives (my, your, his, her, our, their), and Demonstratives (this/that/these/those)
subModules.vocabularyFocus: Family member nouns, positive adjectives to describe people, and household vocabulary

content.summary: Welcome to your Reading Mission! In this lesson, you will read a short, fun passage about a person introducing their family. You will learn to understand sentences about family members, spot possessive forms like 'my,' 'his,' 'her,' and the possessive 's (for example, 'Maria's brother'), and notice how 'this,' 'that,' 'these,' and 'those' are used to point to people and things. By the end, you will feel confident reading simple family descriptions in English. Let's get started!

linguisticTarget.grammar: Possessive 's (e.g., Tom's sister), possessive adjectives (my, your, his, her, its, our, their), and demonstratives (this/that for singular, these/those for plural).
linguisticTarget.vocabulary: Family members (brother, sister, father, mother, grandfather, grandmother, cousin, uncle, aunt), positive adjectives (kind, funny, smart, helpful, friendly, generous), and home-related words (apartment, bedroom, kitchen).
linguisticTarget.readingStrategy: Skimming the passage first to understand the main idea (Who is talking? What is the topic?), then scanning for specific details like names, family relationships, and possessive words.

learningObjectives: Understand the main idea of a short A1 passage about someone's family.
Identify key details including family members' names, relationships, and descriptions.
Recognize possessive 's and possessive adjectives (my, his, her, our, their) in context.
Distinguish between this/that (singular) and these/those (plural) when pointing to people or things.
Use positive adjectives to understand how family members are described.

contextWarmup.prompt: Read this sentence: 'This is my mother. Her name is Sara. She is very kind.' Who is kind?
contextWarmup.explanation: The sentence says 'This is my mother. Her name is Sara. She is very kind.' The word 'She' refers to Sara, the mother. So Sara is the kind person. Great job if you got it right!

rules: Possessive 's: Add 's after a person's name to show that something belongs to them. Example: 'Maria's father' means the father of Maria. When you see a name followed by 's, ask yourself: 'What belongs to this person?'

Possessive adjectives: Use 'my, your, his, her, its, our, their' before a noun to show who owns it. Example: 'her brother' means the brother of a girl or woman. Match the adjective to the person: 'his' = a boy or man, 'her' = a girl or woman.

This/That (singular): Use 'this' for one person or thing that is near you. Use 'that' for one person or thing that is far from you. Example: 'This is my sister' (she is next to me). 'That is my cousin' (he is over there).

These/Those (plural): Use 'these' for two or more people or things that are near you. Use 'those' for two or more people or things that are far from you. Example: 'These are my books' (the books are here). 'Those are her friends' (the friends are over there).
When you read, look for clue words like 'my,' 'his,' 'her,' and names with 's to understand who belongs to whom in a family.

commonTrap.trapTitle: Common Beginner Pitfall: Forgetting the Possessive 's
commonTrap.explanation: Many beginners forget to add 's after a name when showing possession. They write or read 'Tom house' instead of 'Tom's house.' Also, beginners sometimes confuse 'his' (for a boy or man) and 'her' (for a girl or woman). Always check: Is the person male or female? Then choose the correct possessive adjective.
commonTrap.wrong: Tom house is big. / She brother is funny. / William father is kind.
commonTrap.correct: Tom's house is big. / Her brother is funny. / William's father is kind.

content.context: Lucia is a young woman from Brazil. She is writing a short text for her English class about her family. She describes her family members and their home.
content.text:
Hello! My name is Lucia. I'm from Brazil, and this is my family. My father's name is Carlos. He's tall and very kind. My mother's name is Ana. She's smart and funny. I have one brother. His name is Pedro. He's 15 years old. Pedro is really helpful at home.

We live in a big apartment in São Paulo. Our apartment has four bedrooms. This is my bedroom — it's small but nice! That is my brother's bedroom next to mine.

My grandmother's name is Rosa. She's my mother's mother. She is generous and loving. My uncle Antonio is my mother's brother. His wife is my aunt Sofia. She's very friendly. Those are their children — my cousins, Marco and Bianca. These are the people I love. We're a happy family!

highlights.note: 'My' is a possessive adjective. It shows the family belongs to Lucia.
Possessive 's after 'father' shows the name belongs to her father.
'He's' is a contraction of 'He is.' 'Kind' is a positive adjective.
'His' is the possessive adjective for a boy or man.
'Our' is the possessive adjective for 'we.' It shows the apartment belongs to the whole family.
'This' is used because the bedroom is near Lucia (she is pointing to it).
'That' is used because the brother's bedroom is farther away. 'Brother's' uses possessive 's.
Possessive 's after 'grandmother' shows the name belongs to her grandmother.
'Those' is used for plural things/people far away. 'Their' is the possessive adjective for 'they.'

highlights.text: These are the people I love
highlights.note: 'These' is used for plural things/people that are near.
A positive adjective meaning someone likes to give and share.
A positive adjective meaning someone is warm and nice to others.

gistQuestion.prompt: What is the main idea of the passage?
options: Lucia introduces her family members and describes them with positive adjectives.
Lucia talks about her school and her favorite teacher.
Lucia describes her holiday in a new city.
gistQuestion.explanation: The passage is all about Lucia's family. She introduces her father, mother, brother, grandmother, uncle, aunt, and cousins. She also describes them using kind words like 'kind,' 'smart,' 'funny,' and 'friendly.' So the main idea is about her family.

detailQuestions.explanation: The passage says: 'My father's name is Carlos.' The possessive 's after 'father' tells us that the name belongs to Lucia's father. So the answer is Carlos.

detailQuestions.prompt: How many bedrooms does Lucia's apartment have?
detailQuestions.explanation: The passage says: 'Our apartment has four bedrooms.' The possessive adjective 'our' shows the apartment belongs to Lucia's family. The answer is four bedrooms.

detailQuestions.prompt: Who is Rosa in the passage?
detailQuestions.explanation: The passage says: 'My grandmother's name is Rosa. She's my mother's mother.' This tells us Rosa is Lucia's grandmother on her mother's side.

options: Lucia's cousins — the children of her uncle and aunt
detailQuestions.explanation: The passage says: 'Those are their children — my cousins, Marco and Bianca.' The word 'their' refers to Uncle Antonio and Aunt Sofia. So Marco and Bianca are Lucia's cousins.

questions.question: In the passage, Lucia says: 'My mother's name is Ana.' What does the 's after 'mother' mean?
options: It shows possession — the name belongs to her mother.
questions.answer: It shows possession — the name belongs to her mother.
questions.explanation: When we write 'My mother's name,' the 's shows that the name belongs to her mother. This is the possessive 's. It is different from the contraction 'She's' (She is).

questions.question: Lucia writes: 'His name is Pedro.' Who does 'His' refer to?
questions.explanation: Just before this sentence, Lucia says: 'I have one brother.' Then she says: 'His name is Pedro.' The possessive adjective 'His' refers to the brother she just mentioned.

questions.question: Which sentence correctly uses the possessive 's?
questions.explanation: To show that the name belongs to the grandmother, we add 's after 'grandmother.' The correct form is 'My grandmother's name is Rosa.' Without the apostrophe and s, the sentence is grammatically incorrect.

questions.question: Lucia says: 'This is my bedroom.' Why does she use 'this' and not 'that'?
options: Because the bedroom is near her — she is pointing to something close.
Because the bedroom is far away from her.
questions.answer: Because the bedroom is near her — she is pointing to something close.
questions.explanation: We use 'this' for something singular that is near us. Lucia is standing in or next to her bedroom, so she says 'This is my bedroom.' If it were far away, she would say 'That is my bedroom.'

questions.question: Lucia writes: 'Those are their children — my cousins, Marco and Bianca.' Why does she use 'those' instead of 'this'?
options: Because she is talking about more than one person who are not right next to her.
Because she is talking about only one person who is near her.
Because 'those' is used for singular nouns.
questions.answer: Because she is talking about more than one person who are not right next to her.
questions.explanation: 'Those' is used for plural people or things that are farther away. Marco and Bianca are two people (plural), and they are not standing right next to Lucia. So 'those' is the correct word.

questions.question: Which word correctly completes this sentence? '_______ is my aunt Sofia. She's very friendly.'
questions.explanation: We need a singular demonstrative because we are talking about one person (Aunt Sofia). 'Those' and 'These' are for plural. 'That' is correct for one person who is not right next to the speaker.

questions.question: According to the passage, which adjective describes Lucia's brother Pedro?
questions.explanation: The passage says: 'Pedro is really helpful at home.' The adjective 'helpful' describes Pedro. 'Generous' describes the grandmother Rosa, and 'friendly' describes Aunt Sofia.

questions.question: Read this sentence from the passage: 'She's my mother's mother.' What does this sentence tell us about Rosa?
options: Rosa is Lucia's grandmother on her mother's side.
questions.answer: Rosa is Lucia's grandmother on her mother's side.
questions.explanation: The sentence 'She's my mother's mother' means Rosa is the mother of Lucia's mother. That makes Rosa Lucia's grandmother. Notice the two possessive forms: 'my mother's' (belonging to my mother) and 'mother' (the person who is her mother).

content.summary: In this listening mission, you will hear a conversation between three people: Steve, Jane, and Renata. They are meeting for the first time and talking about their families. Pay close attention to possessive words like 'my', 'your', 'her', 'his', 'their', and 'our'. Also listen for family words like 'mother', 'father', 'brothers', 'sisters', and 'parents'. A good strategy is to listen for these key words first, then try to understand the full sentence around them. Remember that in natural speech, words often join together and sounds change slightly.
learningObjectives: Identify family member vocabulary such as mother, father, brothers, sisters, and parents in spoken English.
Recognise possessive adjectives (my, your, his, her, our, their) when used in natural conversation.
Understand simple introductions and descriptions of family members at natural A1 speaking speed.
Distinguish between singular and plural family references such as 'brother' versus 'brothers'.

keyPhrases.note: We use 'this is' to introduce a person who is near us or present with us.

keyPhrases.phrase: She's here on holiday with her mother and father.
keyPhrases.meaning: Dia di sini berlibur bersama ibu dan ayahnya.
keyPhrases.note: Notice the possessive adjective 'her' before 'mother and father' to show they belong to Renata.

keyPhrases.phrase: Have you got any brothers or sisters?
keyPhrases.meaning: Apakah kamu punya saudara laki-laki atau perempuan?
keyPhrases.note: This is a common British English way to ask about siblings. 'Have you got' means the same as 'Do you have'.

keyPhrases.phrase: Their names are Alex and Ricky.
keyPhrases.meaning: Nama mereka adalah Alex dan Ricky.
keyPhrases.note: 'Their' is the possessive adjective for 'they'. It shows the names belong to the two brothers.
'His' is the possessive adjective for 'he'. Here it refers to Renata's father.
'Our' is the possessive adjective for 'we'. Renata uses it to talk about her family's shared language.

connectedSpeech.note: In fast speech, 'name is' contracts to 'name's'. The /ɪz/ sound reduces to just /z/ attached to the previous word.
'What is' contracts to 'What's'. The /t/ and /s/ blend together smoothly. Also 'your' may lose the /r/ sound before a consonant in some accents.
'She is' contracts to 'She's'. The /ɪz/ reduces to /z/ and links directly to the next word.
'I have' contracts to 'I've'. The /h/ in 'have' disappears completely and only the /v/ sound remains.
'That is' contracts to 'That's'. The /ɪz/ reduces to /s/ after the /t/ sound, creating a /ts/ cluster.

sections.title: Audio Dialogue: Meeting Renata and Her Family

content.context: Steve meets Jane and Renata at a social gathering. Renata is from Brazil and is on holiday with her parents. The three of them chat about their families, siblings, and shared interests like football.
content.audioPrompt: Listen carefully to the following dialogue between three speakers. Pay attention to how they talk about family members and use possessive adjectives like my, your, her, his, their, and our.

lines.speaker: Steve
lines.text: Hello. My name's Steve. What's your name?

lines.speaker: Jane
lines.text: Hi, I'm Jane and this is Renata. She's Brazilian. She's here on holiday with her mother and father.
lines.translation: Hai, aku Jane dan ini Renata. Dia orang Brazil. Dia di sini berlibur bersama ibu dan ayahnya.

lines.speaker: Steve
lines.text: Fine, thanks. So, you and your parents are from Brazil?
lines.translation: Baik, terima kasih. Jadi, kamu dan orang tuamu dari Brazil?

lines.speaker: Renata
lines.text: That's right - we speak Portuguese. It's our first language.
lines.translation: Betul - kami berbicara bahasa Portugis. Itu bahasa pertama kami.

lines.speaker: Jane
lines.text: Have you got any brothers or sisters?
lines.translation: Apakah kamu punya saudara laki-laki atau perempuan?

lines.speaker: Jane
lines.text: Yes, I've got two brothers. Their names are Alex and Ricky. They love football! And they love Brazilian football!
lines.translation: Ya, aku punya dua saudara laki-laki. Nama mereka Alex dan Ricky. Mereka suka sepak bola! Dan mereka suka sepak bola Brazil!

lines.speaker: Renata
lines.text: Great! My father is a football fan, too - his favourite team is Flamengo.
lines.translation: Bagus! Ayahku juga penggemar sepak bola - tim favoritnya adalah Flamengo.

content.summary: In this writing lesson, you will learn how to write sentences and short paragraphs about your family. You will practice using possessive 's (like Kate's brother), possessive adjectives (my, your, his, her, our, their), and demonstratives (this, that, these, those). You will also learn to give simple compliments about family members. Follow the blueprint steps below to build strong, correct sentences about the people you love!

blueprintItems.title: Introduce a Family Member
blueprintItems.example: This is my mother. Her name is Sarah.

blueprintItems.title: Show Possession with 's
blueprintItems.example: Anna's father is very kind. William's sister is a student.

blueprintItems.title: Describe a Family Member with a Compliment
blueprintItems.formula: My/His/Her + family member + is + positive adjective.
blueprintItems.example: My grandmother is very beautiful. Her brother is really smart.

blueprintItems.title: Use Demonstratives for Groups
blueprintItems.example: These are my parents. Those are my cousins.

mechanicsRules.rule: Always use a capital letter for names of people.
mechanicsRules.why: Names of people are proper nouns. Proper nouns always start with a capital letter in English.

mechanicsRules.rule: Always start a sentence with a capital letter and end it with a period (.) or question mark (?).
mechanicsRules.why: Every English sentence must begin with a capital letter and end with correct punctuation. This makes your writing clear and correct.

mechanicsRules.rule: Place the apostrophe and 's directly after the owner's name to show possession. Do not add a space before 's.
mechanicsRules.why: The apostrophe + s ('s) must be attached to the name to show that something belongs to that person. A space before 's is incorrect.

mechanicsRules.rule: Use 'this/that' with 'is' for one person or thing, and 'these/those' with 'are' for more than one.
mechanicsRules.why: 'This' and 'that' are singular and go with 'is'. 'These' and 'those' are plural and go with 'are'. Mixing them is a common mistake.

That is Sarah's grandmother. She is very kind.
sampleSentences.id: Itu nenek Sarah. Dia sangat baik hati.

sampleSentences.en: These are my brothers. Their names are Tom and Jack.
sampleSentences.id: Ini saudara-saudara laki-laki saya. Nama mereka Tom dan Jack.

sampleSentences.en: My sister is really beautiful. Her smile is lovely.
sampleSentences.id: Kakak perempuan saya sangat cantik. Senyumnya indah.

sampleSentences.id: Itu orang tua Kevin. Mereka sangat ramah.

mechanicsChallenges.keyRule: Start each sentence with a capital letter. Use an apostrophe + s ('s) directly after the name to show possession. End each sentence with a period.

mechanicsChallenges.keyRule: Do not put spaces or apostrophes in regular plural nouns (cousins, names). Capitalize proper nouns (Lisa, Tom) and the first word of each sentence.

mechanicsChallenges.keyRule: Attach the apostrophe + s ('s) to the owner's name without a space. Start each new sentence with a capital letter and end with a period.

mechanicsChallenges.keyRule: The word 'parents' is a regular plural noun and does not need an apostrophe. Separate two complete ideas into two sentences with proper punctuation.

practicumQuestions.prompt: Write 3 sentences introducing members of your family. Use 'This is' or 'That is' for each person, include a possessive adjective (my, his, her), and mention each person's name.
practicumQuestions.criteria: The response must contain at least 3 complete sentences. Each sentence must start with a capital letter and end with a period. The student must correctly use 'This is' or 'That is', at least one possessive adjective (my, his, her, our, their), and include proper names with capital letters.
practicumQuestions.sampleGoodAnswer: This is my mother. Her name is Clara. That is my brother. His name is Leo. This is my grandmother. Her name is Rosa.

practicumQuestions.prompt: Write 3 sentences using possessive 's to talk about things that belong to your family members. For example, talk about your sister's phone, your father's car, or your mother's smile.
practicumQuestions.criteria: The response must contain at least 3 complete sentences. Each sentence must correctly use possessive 's attached to a person's name or family title (e.g., Maria's, my sister's). Sentences must have correct capitalization and punctuation.
practicumQuestions.sampleGoodAnswer: My mother's cooking is delicious. My father's car is very big. Sarah's room is clean and beautiful.

practicumQuestions.prompt: Write a short paragraph (at least 5 sentences) about your family. Introduce at least two family members using demonstratives (this, that, these, those). Describe their good qualities and give at least two compliments. Use possessive adjectives and possessive 's.
practicumQuestions.criteria: The response must contain at least 5 complete sentences forming a coherent paragraph. The student must correctly use at least one demonstrative (this/that/these/those), at least two possessive adjectives (my, his, her, our, their), at least one possessive 's construction, and at least two compliments using positive adjectives. All sentences must have correct capitalization and end punctuation.
practicumQuestions.sampleGoodAnswer: This is my family. That is my father. His name is Ahmad. He is very strong and kind. This is my mother. Her name is Siti. My mother's smile is very beautiful. These are my sisters. Their names are Rina and Dewi. They are really smart and funny. I love my family very much.

subModules.title: Speaking Lab: Talking About My Family

content.summary: In this speaking lab, you will practise talking about your family members, using possessive 's (my brother's name, my mother's hobby), possessive adjectives (my, his, her, your, their), and demonstratives (this, that, these, those). You will also learn to give simple compliments about people. Focus on clear pronunciation of family vocabulary and natural rising and falling intonation when asking and answering questions about your family.
content.audioGuidance: Pay special attention to the /ð/ sound in 'this', 'that', 'these', 'those', 'mother', 'father', and 'brother'. Place your tongue gently between your teeth and blow air softly. Also practise the possessive 's — say it as a quick /z/ sound after voiced consonants (e.g., 'brother's' = /ˈbrʌðərz/) and as /s/ after voiceless consonants (e.g., 'parent's' = /ˈpeərənts/). Use falling intonation for statements like 'This is my sister.' and rising intonation for yes/no questions like 'Is that your father?'

pillars.name: Family Vocabulary Clarity
pillars.target: Pronounce family member words clearly and accurately
pillars.explanation: Practise saying words like 'mother', 'father', 'brother', 'sister', 'grandmother', 'grandfather', 'daughter', 'son', 'husband', and 'wife'. Make sure each syllable is clear. For example, 'grandmother' has three syllables: GRAND-mo-ther.

pillars.name: Possessive 's Articulation
pillars.target: Produce the possessive 's ending naturally in connected speech
pillars.explanation: When you say 'my mother's name' or 'my brother's hobby', the 's after the apostrophe should flow smoothly into the next word. Do not pause between the possessive 's and the following noun. Say 'my mother's name' as one phrase, not three separate words.

pillars.name: Demonstrative Pronunciation
pillars.target: Correctly produce the /ð/ sound in this, that, these, those
pillars.explanation: Many learners replace /ð/ with /d/ or /t/. Remember: 'this' is /ðɪs/, not /dɪs/. 'That' is /ðæt/, not /dæt/. Place your tongue tip between your upper and lower teeth and let the air flow over it gently.

pillars.name: Compliment Intonation
pillars.target: Use warm, natural intonation when giving compliments
pillars.explanation: When you give a compliment like 'Your sister is very kind!' or 'That is a beautiful family!', your voice should rise slightly on the adjective (kind, beautiful) and then fall at the end. This makes your compliment sound sincere and friendly.

stressPairs.shiftExplanation: In 'mother', the stress is on the first syllable: MO-ther. In 'grandmother', the stress moves to the prefix: GRAND-mother. The word 'mother' inside 'grandmother' becomes unstressed. Practise saying both words to feel the rhythm change.
Just like 'grandmother', in 'grandfather' the stress is on the first syllable: GRAND-fa-ther. The word 'father' loses its primary stress when it becomes part of the compound word.
In 'sister', the stress is on 'SIS'. In 'stepsister', the primary stress shifts to the prefix 'STEP', and 'sister' carries secondary or no stress. This is common in compound family words.
In 'brother', the stress is on 'BRO'. In 'stepbrother', the primary stress is on 'STEP'. Notice how compound family words always stress the first part of the compound.

drills.targetText: This is my mother. Her name is Sari.
drills.phonetic: /ðɪs ɪz maɪ ˈmʌðər. hɜːr neɪm ɪz ˈsɑːri/
drills.focus: Possessive adjective 'my' and 'her' with /ð/ in 'this' and 'mother'
drills.hint: Make sure your tongue touches between your teeth for the 'th' sounds in 'this' and 'mother'. Keep 'my' and 'her' short and unstressed.

drills.targetText: My brother's name is Ahmad. He is very kind.
drills.phonetic: /maɪ ˈbrʌðərz neɪm ɪz ɑːˈmæd. hiː ɪz ˈveri kaɪnd/
drills.hint: Say 'brother's name' as one smooth phrase. The possessive 's sounds like /z/. Stress the word 'kind' at the end of the sentence.

drills.targetText: That is my father. He is tall and helpful.
drills.phonetic: /ðæt ɪz maɪ ˈfɑːðər. hiː ɪz tɔːl ænd ˈhelpfʊl/
drills.hint: Start with the /ð/ sound in 'that'. Let your voice fall at the end of each sentence because these are statements, not questions.

drills.targetText: These are my grandparents. They are very nice.
drills.phonetic: /ðiːz ɑːr maɪ ˈɡrænpeərənts. ðeɪ ɑːr ˈveri naɪs/
drills.focus: Plural demonstrative 'these' and possessive 'my' with family vocabulary
drills.hint: The word 'these' has a long /iː/ vowel and a /z/ at the end. 'Grandparents' has the stress on 'GRAND'. Say it clearly: GRAND-par-ents.

drills.targetText: Is that your sister? She is really beautiful!
drills.phonetic: /ɪz ðæt jɔːr ˈsɪstər? ʃiː ɪz ˈrɪəli ˈbjuːtɪfʊl/
drills.focus: Rising intonation for yes/no question and compliment delivery
drills.hint: Your voice should rise at the end of 'Is that your sister?' because it is a yes/no question. Then use warm, falling intonation on the compliment 'She is really beautiful!'

drills.targetText: My mother's favourite hobby is cooking.
drills.hint: Connect 'mother's favourite' smoothly. Do not pause after the possessive 's. Stress 'favourite' on the first syllable: FAV-our-ite.

roleplay.context: You are at a family gathering. Mr. Khoirul, a friendly English teacher, visits your home and asks about your family members. You introduce each family member, describe their good qualities, and use possessive forms and demonstratives naturally. This is a warm, casual conversation.

turns.text: Hello! Tell me about your family. Have you got any brothers or sisters?
turns.translation: Halo! Ceritakan tentang keluargamu. Apakah kamu punya saudara laki-laki atau perempuan?

turns.speaker: You
turns.text: Yes, I have one brother. His name is Ahmad.
turns.translation: Ya, saya punya satu saudara laki-laki. Namanya Ahmad.

turns.speaker: Mr. Khoirul
turns.text: That's nice! What is your brother like? Can you describe him with a good adjective?
turns.translation: Bagus! Seperti apa saudaramu? Bisakah kamu mendeskripsikannya dengan kata sifat yang baik?

turns.speaker: You
turns.text: He is very kind and helpful. He always helps me with my homework.
turns.translation: Dia sangat baik dan suka menolong. Dia selalu membantu saya dengan PR saya.

turns.speaker: Mr. Khoirul
turns.text: Wonderful! And what about your parents? Where are they from?
turns.translation: Luar biasa! Bagaimana dengan orang tuamu? Dari mana mereka berasal?

turns.speaker: You
turns.text: My mother and father are from Indonesia. My mother's favourite hobby is cooking.
turns.translation: Ibu dan ayah saya dari Indonesia. Hobi favorit ibu saya adalah memasak.

turns.speaker: Mr. Khoirul

turns.translation: Bagus sekali! Sekarang, bisakah kamu ceritakan tentang rumahmu? Apa ruangan favoritmu?

turns.speaker: You
turns.text: My favourite room is my bedroom. It is really nice and comfortable.
turns.translation: Ruangan favorit saya adalah kamar tidur saya. Kamar itu sangat bagus dan nyaman.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Tell a short story about your family. Introduce your family members, say their names, and describe one good quality for each person. Use possessive 's and possessive adjectives (my, his, her). Speak for about 30 seconds.
practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: Now it is your turn to tell me about your family. Please introduce at least three family members. Tell me their names and say something nice about each person. Use words like 'my', 'his', 'her', and possessive 's. For example, 'My sister's name is Ani. She is very clever.' Ready? Go ahead!
storyPoints: Introduce at least three family members by their relationship to you (for example: my mother, my father, my sister).
Use possessive 's to talk about each person's name or quality (for example: my brother's name, my father's job).
Describe one good quality for each family member using a simple adjective (for example: kind, helpful, clever, funny).
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: My mother's name is Sari. She is very kind. My father's name is Budi. He is very helpful. My sister's name is Ani. She is really clever.
practicumQuestions.phonetic: /maɪ ˈmʌðərz neɪm ɪz ˈsɑːri. ʃiː ɪz ˈveri kaɪnd. maɪ ˈfɑːðərz neɪm ɪz ˈbuːdi. hiː ɪz ˈveri ˈhelpfʊl. maɪ ˈsɪstərz neɪm ɪz ˈɑːni. ʃiː ɪz ˈrɪəli ˈklevər/
practicumQuestions.hint: Remember to use possessive 's after the family member word: 'my mother's name', not 'my mother name'. Use falling intonation at the end of each statement.
practicumQuestions.explanation: This storytelling task practises introducing family members using possessive 's (my mother's name) and possessive adjectives (my, his, her). It also practises using simple adjectives to describe people's good qualities, which is a key objective of this unit.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Describe your family using demonstratives (this, that, these, those). Imagine you are showing a family photo to a friend. Point to each person and say who they are and what they are like.
practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: Imagine you have a family photo. You are showing it to me. Please point to the people in the photo and tell me who they are. Use words like 'this is', 'that is', 'these are', and 'those are'. Describe each person with a nice adjective. Ready? Start now!
storyPoints: Use 'this is' or 'that is' to introduce individual family members in the photo.
Use 'these are' or 'those are' to introduce groups of family members (for example: these are my grandparents).
Give a simple compliment or describe a good quality for at least two people in the photo.
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: This is my mother. She is very beautiful. That is my father. He is really strong. These are my grandparents. They are very kind and loving.
practicumQuestions.phonetic: /ðɪs ɪz maɪ ˈmʌðər. ʃiː ɪz ˈveri ˈbjuːtɪfʊl. ðæt ɪz maɪ ˈfɑːðər. hiː ɪz ˈrɪəli strɒŋ. ðiːz ɑːr maɪ ˈɡrænpeərənts. ðeɪ ɑːr ˈveri kaɪnd ænd ˈlʌvɪŋ/
practicumQuestions.hint: Remember the /ð/ sound at the beginning of 'this', 'that', 'these', and 'those'. Place your tongue between your teeth. Use falling intonation for statements.
practicumQuestions.explanation: This task practises using demonstratives (this/that/these/those) to identify family members, combined with possessive adjectives and simple compliment adjectives. It reinforces the unit's focus on describing family and giving compliments.

practicumQuestions.instruction: You receive a video call from Mr. Khoirul. He wants to meet your family. Introduce your family members one by one. Use possessive 's and possessive adjectives.
practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: Ring ring! Hello, this is Mr. Khoirul calling! I would love to meet your family today. Can you introduce them to me one by one? Tell me their names and something nice about each person.
practicumQuestions.scenarioContext: You are at home with your family. Mr. Khoirul, your English teacher, calls you on a video call. He is very friendly and curious about your family. You need to introduce your mother, father, and one sibling. For each person, say their name using possessive 's and describe one good quality.
practicumQuestions.characterRole: Mr. Khoirul is a warm and encouraging English teacher. He asks simple follow-up questions like 'What is his name?' and 'Is she kind?' He speaks slowly and clearly at A1 level.
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: This is my mother. Her name is Sari. She is very kind. This is my father. His name is Budi. He is really helpful.
practicumQuestions.phonetic: /ðɪs ɪz maɪ ˈmʌðər. hɜːr neɪm ɪz ˈsɑːri. ʃiː ɪz ˈveri kaɪnd. ðɪs ɪz maɪ ˈfɑːðər. hɪz neɪm ɪz ˈbuːdi. hiː ɪz ˈrɪəli ˈhelpfʊl/
practicumQuestions.hint: When Mr. Khoirul asks 'What is her name?', answer with a full sentence: 'Her name is...' Do not just say the name alone.
practicumQuestions.explanation: This roleplay practises real-time family introductions using possessive adjectives (my, his, her) and possessive 's in a natural conversation with a teacher.

practicumQuestions.instruction: You are at school. A new classmate asks about your family. Answer the questions and ask about their family too. Use possessive adjectives and give compliments.
practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: Hi! I am new in this class. My name is Rina. I want to know about your family. How many people are in your family? Tell me about them!
practicumQuestions.scenarioContext: It is your first day back at school. A new student named Rina sits next to you. She is friendly and wants to get to know you. She asks about your family members, and you also ask about hers. You practise using possessive adjectives (my, your, his, her) and giving simple compliments.
practicumQuestions.characterRole: Rina is a cheerful new classmate. She speaks simple English and asks questions like 'How many brothers do you have?' and 'What is your mother like?' She also shares information about her own family so you can respond with compliments.
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: I have four people in my family. My father is a teacher. My mother is very kind. Your family sounds really nice!
practicumQuestions.phonetic: /aɪ hæv fɔːr ˈpiːpəl ɪn maɪ ˈfæməli. maɪ ˈfɑːðər ɪz ə ˈtiːtʃər. maɪ ˈmʌðər ɪz ˈveri kaɪnd. jɔːr ˈfæməli saʊndz ˈrɪəli naɪs/
practicumQuestions.hint: When Rina tells you about her family, respond with a compliment. For example: 'Your brother sounds very kind!' or 'That is really nice!'
practicumQuestions.explanation: This roleplay practises two-way conversation about families, using possessive adjectives for both 'my' and 'your' family, and giving compliments to a peer.

practicumQuestions.instruction: You are showing your family photo album to Mr. Khoirul. Use demonstratives (this, that, these, those) to point to people in the photos and describe them.
practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: Oh, what a lovely photo album! Can you show me the photos? Please point to each person and tell me who they are. Use 'this is' for people close to you and 'that is' for people far away in the photo.
practicumQuestions.scenarioContext: You are sitting with Mr. Khoirul and looking at your family photo album together. Some photos show people close up (use 'this') and some show people far away or in old photos (use 'that'). Group photos require 'these are' or 'those are'. Describe each person with a positive adjective.
practicumQuestions.characterRole: Mr. Khoirul is looking at the photos with great interest. He asks questions like 'Who is this?' and 'Are those your cousins?' He encourages you to use full sentences and give compliments about the people in the photos.
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: This is my sister. She is very clever. That is my grandfather. He is really funny. These are my cousins. They are very friendly.
practicumQuestions.phonetic: /ðɪs ɪz maɪ ˈsɪstər. ʃiː ɪz ˈveri ˈklevər. ðæt ɪz maɪ ˈɡrænfɑːðər. hiː ɪz ˈrɪəli ˈfʌni. ðiːz ɑːr maɪ ˈkʌzənz. ðeɪ ɑːr ˈveri ˈfrendli/
practicumQuestions.hint: Use 'this is' for one person near you, 'that is' for one person far away, 'these are' for a group near you, and 'those are' for a group far away. Always follow with a description.
practicumQuestions.explanation: This roleplay specifically targets demonstrative pronouns (this/that/these/those) in the context of describing family members, combining them with possessive adjectives and compliment adjectives.

practicumQuestions.instruction: You meet Mr. Khoirul at a school event. He introduces his family to you. Listen, respond politely, and then introduce your own family. Give compliments about his family members.
practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: Hello! Welcome to the school event! I want to introduce my family to you. This is my wife. Her name is Dewi. She is a doctor. And this is my son. His name is Rafi. He is ten years old. Now, can you tell me about your family too?
practicumQuestions.scenarioContext: You are at a school family day event. Mr. Khoirul introduces his wife and son to you. You need to respond with polite compliments about his family, and then introduce your own family members using possessive 's and possessive adjectives. This is a polite, semi-formal conversation.
practicumQuestions.characterRole: Mr. Khoirul is proud of his family and introduces them warmly. He expects you to give a compliment about his wife or son, and then share about your own family. He may ask follow-up questions like 'What does your father do?' or 'Is your sister older or younger?'
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: Nice to meet your family! Your wife is very kind. Your son is really smart. This is my mother. Her name is Sari. She is a wonderful cook.
practicumQuestions.phonetic: /naɪs tuː miːt jɔːr ˈfæməli. jɔːr waɪf ɪz ˈveri kaɪnd. jɔːr sʌn ɪz ˈrɪəli smɑːrt. ðɪs ɪz maɪ ˈmʌðər. hɜːr neɪm ɪz ˈsɑːri. ʃiː ɪz ə ˈwʌndərfʊl kʊk/
practicumQuestions.hint: When someone introduces their family, always respond with a compliment first. Say 'Nice to meet your family!' or 'Your son is very smart!' before talking about your own family.
practicumQuestions.explanation: This roleplay practises both receiving and giving family introductions, using 'your' for the other person's family and 'my/her/his' for your own. It also practises giving polite compliments in a semi-formal setting.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Say the following family vocabulary words clearly. Focus on correct pronunciation of each word.
practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: Let us practise family vocabulary. I will give you a word and you need to say it clearly. Ready? Please say the word: 'grandmother'.
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: grandmother
practicumQuestions.phonetic: /ˈɡrænmʌðər/
practicumQuestions.hint: This word has three syllables: GRAND-mo-ther. The stress is on the first syllable 'GRAND'. Make sure you pronounce the /ð/ sound in 'ther' by placing your tongue between your teeth.
practicumQuestions.explanation: The word 'grandmother' is a compound family noun. At A1 level, learners need to master basic family vocabulary with correct syllable stress. The primary stress falls on 'GRAND', and the /ð/ in the final syllable is a key pronunciation target for this unit.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Say the following sentence aloud. Pay attention to the correct use of possessive 's and the possessive adjective 'her'.
practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: Now let us practise grammar in speaking. Please say this sentence clearly: 'My sister's favourite colour is blue. Her room is blue too.'
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: My sister's favourite colour is blue. Her room is blue too.
practicumQuestions.phonetic: /maɪ ˈsɪstərz ˈfeɪvərɪt ˈkʌlər ɪz bluː. hɜːr ruːm ɪz bluː tuː/
practicumQuestions.hint: Notice two possessive forms here: 'sister's' uses apostrophe s to show that the favourite colour belongs to your sister. 'Her' is a possessive adjective that replaces 'my sister's' to avoid repetition. Say 'sister's favourite' as one smooth phrase.
practicumQuestions.explanation: This drill targets two key grammar points from the unit: possessive 's (sister's favourite) and possessive adjectives (her room). Learners must produce both forms correctly in connected speech, showing they understand that 'her' refers back to 'my sister'.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Say both words and notice how the syllable stress changes. First say 'brother', then say 'stepbrother'. Pay attention to which syllable is strongest.
practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: Let us practise syllable stress with family words. First, say 'brother' — the stress is on 'BRO'. Now say 'stepbrother' — the stress moves to 'STEP'. Say both words: 'BRO-ther' and then 'STEP-bro-ther'. Can you feel the difference?
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: brother, stepbrother
practicumQuestions.phonetic: /ˈbrʌðər/ → /ˈstepbrʌðər/
practicumQuestions.hint: In 'brother', you stress the first syllable: BRO-ther. In 'stepbrother', the stress shifts to the prefix: STEP-bro-ther. The syllable 'bro' becomes weaker in the compound word. Tap your hand on the table on the stressed syllable to feel the rhythm.
practicumQuestions.explanation: This drill practises syllable stress shift in compound family nouns. When 'brother' stands alone, it has primary stress on 'BRO'. When it becomes part of the compound 'stepbrother', the primary stress shifts to the prefix 'STEP', and 'brother' receives reduced stress. This pattern applies to many compound family words (grandmother, grandfather, stepsister).

practicumQuestions.instruction: Say these two sentences with the correct intonation pattern. The first sentence is a yes/no question (rising intonation). The second sentence is a statement with a compliment (falling intonation).
practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: Let us practise intonation. First, say this question with rising intonation — your voice goes UP at the end: 'Is that your sister?' Now say this compliment with falling intonation — your voice goes DOWN at the end: 'She is really beautiful!' Try both sentences now.
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: Is that your sister? She is really beautiful!
practicumQuestions.phonetic: /ɪz ðæt jɔːr ˈsɪstər↗ ʃiː ɪz ˈrɪəli ˈbjuːtɪfʊl↘/
practicumQuestions.hint: For the question 'Is that your sister?', imagine your voice is climbing stairs — it goes UP at the end. For the compliment 'She is really beautiful!', imagine your voice is going down a slide — it goes DOWN at the end. The rising tone shows you are asking; the falling tone shows you are making a warm statement.
practicumQuestions.explanation: This drill contrasts rising intonation (used in yes/no questions like 'Is that your sister?') with falling intonation (used in statements and compliments like 'She is really beautiful!'). Mastering this contrast is essential for natural English conversation about family, especially when asking about and complimenting family members.

reading.question: In the passage, Lucia says: 'My mother's name is Ana.' What does the 's after 'mother' mean?
options: It shows possession — the name belongs to her mother.
reading.answer: It shows possession — the name belongs to her mother.
reading.explanation: When we write 'My mother's name,' the 's shows that the name belongs to her mother. This is the possessive 's. It is different from the contraction 'She's' (She is).

reading.question: Lucia writes: 'His name is Pedro.' Who does 'His' refer to?
reading.explanation: Just before this sentence, Lucia says: 'I have one brother.' Then she says: 'His name is Pedro.' The possessive adjective 'His' refers to the brother she just mentioned.

reading.question: Which sentence correctly uses the possessive 's?
reading.explanation: To show that the name belongs to the grandmother, we add 's after 'grandmother.' The correct form is 'My grandmother's name is Rosa.' Without the apostrophe and s, the sentence is grammatically incorrect.

reading.question: Lucia says: 'This is my bedroom.' Why does she use 'this' and not 'that'?
options: Because the bedroom is near her — she is pointing to something close.
Because the bedroom is far away from her.
reading.answer: Because the bedroom is near her — she is pointing to something close.
reading.explanation: We use 'this' for something singular that is near us. Lucia is standing in or next to her bedroom, so she says 'This is my bedroom.' If it were far away, she would say 'That is my bedroom.'

reading.question: Lucia writes: 'Those are their children — my cousins, Marco and Bianca.' Why does she use 'those' instead of 'this'?
options: Because she is talking about more than one person who are not right next to her.
Because she is talking about only one person who is near her.
Because 'those' is used for singular nouns.
reading.answer: Because she is talking about more than one person who are not right next to her.
reading.explanation: 'Those' is used for plural people or things that are farther away. Marco and Bianca are two people (plural), and they are not standing right next to Lucia. So 'those' is the correct word.

reading.question: Which word correctly completes this sentence? '_______ is my aunt Sofia. She's very friendly.'
reading.explanation: We need a singular demonstrative because we are talking about one person (Aunt Sofia). 'Those' and 'These' are for plural. 'That' is correct for one person who is not right next to the speaker.

reading.question: According to the passage, which adjective describes Lucia's brother Pedro?
reading.explanation: The passage says: 'Pedro is really helpful at home.' The adjective 'helpful' describes Pedro. 'Generous' describes the grandmother Rosa, and 'friendly' describes Aunt Sofia.

reading.question: Read this sentence from the passage: 'She's my mother's mother.' What does this sentence tell us about Rosa?
options: Rosa is Lucia's grandmother on her mother's side.
reading.answer: Rosa is Lucia's grandmother on her mother's side.
reading.explanation: The sentence 'She's my mother's mother' means Rosa is the mother of Lucia's mother. That makes Rosa Lucia's grandmother. Notice the two possessive forms: 'my mother's' (belonging to my mother) and 'mother' (the person who is her mother).

reading.question: Which sentence expresses a future plan?
options: I am going to visit my grandmother tomorrow.
I visit my grandmother every day.
reading.answer: I am going to visit my grandmother tomorrow.
reading.explanation: 'Be going to' expresses a planned future intention.

reading.question: What can you buy at a pharmacy?
reading.explanation: Pharmacies specialize in dispensing medicines and healthcare supplies.

reading.question: Choose the correct pronoun: 'David called Sarah and gave _____ the book.'
reading.explanation: 'Sarah' is female and functions as an object pronoun, which is 'her'.

reading.question: What is the weather like when it is raining?
reading.explanation: Rain brings water, making the weather and ground wet.

reading.question: Choose the correct form: 'They _____ playing football right now.'
reading.explanation: 'They' requires the plural auxiliary 'are' in present continuous.

reading.question: What is Jamie's nationality?
reading.explanation: Jamie is from Spain, so his nationality is Spanish.

writing.prompt: Write 3 sentences introducing members of your family. Use 'This is' or 'That is' for each person, include a possessive adjective (my, his, her), and mention each person's name.
writing.criteria: The response must contain at least 3 complete sentences. Each sentence must start with a capital letter and end with a period. The student must correctly use 'This is' or 'That is', at least one possessive adjective (my, his, her, our, their), and include proper names with capital letters.
writing.sampleGoodAnswer: This is my mother. Her name is Clara. That is my brother. His name is Leo. This is my grandmother. Her name is Rosa.

writing.prompt: Write 3 sentences using possessive 's to talk about things that belong to your family members. For example, talk about your sister's phone, your father's car, or your mother's smile.
writing.criteria: The response must contain at least 3 complete sentences. Each sentence must correctly use possessive 's attached to a person's name or family title (e.g., Maria's, my sister's). Sentences must have correct capitalization and punctuation.
writing.sampleGoodAnswer: My mother's cooking is delicious. My father's car is very big. Sarah's room is clean and beautiful.

writing.prompt: Write a short paragraph (at least 5 sentences) about your family. Introduce at least two family members using demonstratives (this, that, these, those). Describe their good qualities and give at least two compliments. Use possessive adjectives and possessive 's.
writing.criteria: The response must contain at least 5 complete sentences forming a coherent paragraph. The student must correctly use at least one demonstrative (this/that/these/those), at least two possessive adjectives (my, his, her, our, their), at least one possessive 's construction, and at least two compliments using positive adjectives. All sentences must have correct capitalization and end punctuation.
writing.sampleGoodAnswer: This is my family. That is my father. His name is Ahmad. He is very strong and kind. This is my mother. Her name is Siti. My mother's smile is very beautiful. These are my sisters. Their names are Rina and Dewi. They are really smart and funny. I love my family very much.

speaking.instruction: Tell a short story about your family. Introduce your family members, say their names, and describe one good quality for each person. Use possessive 's and possessive adjectives (my, his, her). Speak for about 30 seconds.
speaking.audioPrompt: Now it is your turn to tell me about your family. Please introduce at least three family members. Tell me their names and say something nice about each person. Use words like 'my', 'his', 'her', and possessive 's. For example, 'My sister's name is Ani. She is very clever.' Ready? Go ahead!
storyPoints: Introduce at least three family members by their relationship to you (for example: my mother, my father, my sister).
Use possessive 's to talk about each person's name or quality (for example: my brother's name, my father's job).
Describe one good quality for each family member using a simple adjective (for example: kind, helpful, clever, funny).
speaking.targetSentence: My mother's name is Sari. She is very kind. My father's name is Budi. He is very helpful. My sister's name is Ani. She is really clever.
speaking.phonetic: /maɪ ˈmʌðərz neɪm ɪz ˈsɑːri. ʃiː ɪz ˈveri kaɪnd. maɪ ˈfɑːðərz neɪm ɪz ˈbuːdi. hiː ɪz ˈveri ˈhelpfʊl. maɪ ˈsɪstərz neɪm ɪz ˈɑːni. ʃiː ɪz ˈrɪəli ˈklevər/
speaking.hint: Remember to use possessive 's after the family member word: 'my mother's name', not 'my mother name'. Use falling intonation at the end of each statement.
speaking.explanation: This storytelling task practises introducing family members using possessive 's (my mother's name) and possessive adjectives (my, his, her). It also practises using simple adjectives to describe people's good qualities, which is a key objective of this unit.

speaking.instruction: Describe your family using demonstratives (this, that, these, those). Imagine you are showing a family photo to a friend. Point to each person and say who they are and what they are like.
speaking.audioPrompt: Imagine you have a family photo. You are showing it to me. Please point to the people in the photo and tell me who they are. Use words like 'this is', 'that is', 'these are', and 'those are'. Describe each person with a nice adjective. Ready? Start now!
storyPoints: Use 'this is' or 'that is' to introduce individual family members in the photo.
Use 'these are' or 'those are' to introduce groups of family members (for example: these are my grandparents).
Give a simple compliment or describe a good quality for at least two people in the photo.
speaking.targetSentence: This is my mother. She is very beautiful. That is my father. He is really strong. These are my grandparents. They are very kind and loving.
speaking.phonetic: /ðɪs ɪz maɪ ˈmʌðər. ʃiː ɪz ˈveri ˈbjuːtɪfʊl. ðæt ɪz maɪ ˈfɑːðər. hiː ɪz ˈrɪəli strɒŋ. ðiːz ɑːr maɪ ˈɡrænpeərənts. ðeɪ ɑːr ˈveri kaɪnd ænd ˈlʌvɪŋ/
speaking.hint: Remember the /ð/ sound at the beginning of 'this', 'that', 'these', and 'those'. Place your tongue between your teeth. Use falling intonation for statements.
speaking.explanation: This task practises using demonstratives (this/that/these/those) to identify family members, combined with possessive adjectives and simple compliment adjectives. It reinforces the unit's focus on describing family and giving compliments.

speaking.instruction: You receive a video call from Mr. Khoirul. He wants to meet your family. Introduce your family members one by one. Use possessive 's and possessive adjectives.
speaking.audioPrompt: Ring ring! Hello, this is Mr. Khoirul calling! I would love to meet your family today. Can you introduce them to me one by one? Tell me their names and something nice about each person.
speaking.scenarioContext: You are at home with your family. Mr. Khoirul, your English teacher, calls you on a video call. He is very friendly and curious about your family. You need to introduce your mother, father, and one sibling. For each person, say their name using possessive 's and describe one good quality.
speaking.characterRole: Mr. Khoirul is a warm and encouraging English teacher. He asks simple follow-up questions like 'What is his name?' and 'Is she kind?' He speaks slowly and clearly at A1 level.
speaking.targetSentence: This is my mother. Her name is Sari. She is very kind. This is my father. His name is Budi. He is really helpful.
speaking.phonetic: /ðɪs ɪz maɪ ˈmʌðər. hɜːr neɪm ɪz ˈsɑːri. ʃiː ɪz ˈveri kaɪnd. ðɪs ɪz maɪ ˈfɑːðər. hɪz neɪm ɪz ˈbuːdi. hiː ɪz ˈrɪəli ˈhelpfʊl/
speaking.hint: When Mr. Khoirul asks 'What is her name?', answer with a full sentence: 'Her name is...' Do not just say the name alone.
speaking.explanation: This roleplay practises real-time family introductions using possessive adjectives (my, his, her) and possessive 's in a natural conversation with a teacher.

speaking.instruction: You are at school. A new classmate asks about your family. Answer the questions and ask about their family too. Use possessive adjectives and give compliments.
speaking.audioPrompt: Hi! I am new in this class. My name is Rina. I want to know about your family. How many people are in your family? Tell me about them!
speaking.scenarioContext: It is your first day back at school. A new student named Rina sits next to you. She is friendly and wants to get to know you. She asks about your family members, and you also ask about hers. You practise using possessive adjectives (my, your, his, her) and giving simple compliments.
speaking.characterRole: Rina is a cheerful new classmate. She speaks simple English and asks questions like 'How many brothers do you have?' and 'What is your mother like?' She also shares information about her own family so you can respond with compliments.
speaking.targetSentence: I have four people in my family. My father is a teacher. My mother is very kind. Your family sounds really nice!
speaking.phonetic: /aɪ hæv fɔːr ˈpiːpəl ɪn maɪ ˈfæməli. maɪ ˈfɑːðər ɪz ə ˈtiːtʃər. maɪ ˈmʌðər ɪz ˈveri kaɪnd. jɔːr ˈfæməli saʊndz ˈrɪəli naɪs/
speaking.hint: When Rina tells you about her family, respond with a compliment. For example: 'Your brother sounds very kind!' or 'That is really nice!'
speaking.explanation: This roleplay practises two-way conversation about families, using possessive adjectives for both 'my' and 'your' family, and giving compliments to a peer.

speaking.instruction: You are showing your family photo album to Mr. Khoirul. Use demonstratives (this, that, these, those) to point to people in the photos and describe them.
speaking.audioPrompt: Oh, what a lovely photo album! Can you show me the photos? Please point to each person and tell me who they are. Use 'this is' for people close to you and 'that is' for people far away in the photo.
speaking.scenarioContext: You are sitting with Mr. Khoirul and looking at your family photo album together. Some photos show people close up (use 'this') and some show people far away or in old photos (use 'that'). Group photos require 'these are' or 'those are'. Describe each person with a positive adjective.
speaking.characterRole: Mr. Khoirul is looking at the photos with great interest. He asks questions like 'Who is this?' and 'Are those your cousins?' He encourages you to use full sentences and give compliments about the people in the photos.
speaking.targetSentence: This is my sister. She is very clever. That is my grandfather. He is really funny. These are my cousins. They are very friendly.
speaking.phonetic: /ðɪs ɪz maɪ ˈsɪstər. ʃiː ɪz ˈveri ˈklevər. ðæt ɪz maɪ ˈɡrænfɑːðər. hiː ɪz ˈrɪəli ˈfʌni. ðiːz ɑːr maɪ ˈkʌzənz. ðeɪ ɑːr ˈveri ˈfrendli/
speaking.hint: Use 'this is' for one person near you, 'that is' for one person far away, 'these are' for a group near you, and 'those are' for a group far away. Always follow with a description.
speaking.explanation: This roleplay specifically targets demonstrative pronouns (this/that/these/those) in the context of describing family members, combining them with possessive adjectives and compliment adjectives.

speaking.instruction: You meet Mr. Khoirul at a school event. He introduces his family to you. Listen, respond politely, and then introduce your own family. Give compliments about his family members.
speaking.audioPrompt: Hello! Welcome to the school event! I want to introduce my family to you. This is my wife. Her name is Dewi. She is a doctor. And this is my son. His name is Rafi. He is ten years old. Now, can you tell me about your family too?
speaking.scenarioContext: You are at a school family day event. Mr. Khoirul introduces his wife and son to you. You need to respond with polite compliments about his family, and then introduce your own family members using possessive 's and possessive adjectives. This is a polite, semi-formal conversation.
speaking.characterRole: Mr. Khoirul is proud of his family and introduces them warmly. He expects you to give a compliment about his wife or son, and then share about your own family. He may ask follow-up questions like 'What does your father do?' or 'Is your sister older or younger?'
speaking.targetSentence: Nice to meet your family! Your wife is very kind. Your son is really smart. This is my mother. Her name is Sari. She is a wonderful cook.
speaking.phonetic: /naɪs tuː miːt jɔːr ˈfæməli. jɔːr waɪf ɪz ˈveri kaɪnd. jɔːr sʌn ɪz ˈrɪəli smɑːrt. ðɪs ɪz maɪ ˈmʌðər. hɜːr neɪm ɪz ˈsɑːri. ʃiː ɪz ə ˈwʌndərfʊl kʊk/
speaking.hint: When someone introduces their family, always respond with a compliment first. Say 'Nice to meet your family!' or 'Your son is very smart!' before talking about your own family.
speaking.explanation: This roleplay practises both receiving and giving family introductions, using 'your' for the other person's family and 'my/her/his' for your own. It also practises giving polite compliments in a semi-formal setting.

speaking.instruction: Say the following family vocabulary words clearly. Focus on correct pronunciation of each word.
speaking.audioPrompt: Let us practise family vocabulary. I will give you a word and you need to say it clearly. Ready? Please say the word: 'grandmother'.
speaking.hint: This word has three syllables: GRAND-mo-ther. The stress is on the first syllable 'GRAND'. Make sure you pronounce the /ð/ sound in 'ther' by placing your tongue between your teeth.
speaking.explanation: The word 'grandmother' is a compound family noun. At A1 level, learners need to master basic family vocabulary with correct syllable stress. The primary stress falls on 'GRAND', and the /ð/ in the final syllable is a key pronunciation target for this unit.

speaking.instruction: Say the following sentence aloud. Pay attention to the correct use of possessive 's and the possessive adjective 'her'.
speaking.audioPrompt: Now let us practise grammar in speaking. Please say this sentence clearly: 'My sister's favourite colour is blue. Her room is blue too.'
speaking.targetSentence: My sister's favourite colour is blue. Her room is blue too.
speaking.phonetic: /maɪ ˈsɪstərz ˈfeɪvərɪt ˈkʌlər ɪz bluː. hɜːr ruːm ɪz bluː tuː/
speaking.hint: Notice two possessive forms here: 'sister's' uses apostrophe s to show that the favourite colour belongs to your sister. 'Her' is a possessive adjective that replaces 'my sister's' to avoid repetition. Say 'sister's favourite' as one smooth phrase.
speaking.explanation: This drill targets two key grammar points from the unit: possessive 's (sister's favourite) and possessive adjectives (her room). Learners must produce both forms correctly in connected speech, showing they understand that 'her' refers back to 'my sister'.

speaking.instruction: Say both words and notice how the syllable stress changes. First say 'brother', then say 'stepbrother'. Pay attention to which syllable is strongest.
speaking.audioPrompt: Let us practise syllable stress with family words. First, say 'brother' — the stress is on 'BRO'. Now say 'stepbrother' — the stress moves to 'STEP'. Say both words: 'BRO-ther' and then 'STEP-bro-ther'. Can you feel the difference?
speaking.hint: In 'brother', you stress the first syllable: BRO-ther. In 'stepbrother', the stress shifts to the prefix: STEP-bro-ther. The syllable 'bro' becomes weaker in the compound word. Tap your hand on the table on the stressed syllable to feel the rhythm.
speaking.explanation: This drill practises syllable stress shift in compound family nouns. When 'brother' stands alone, it has primary stress on 'BRO'. When it becomes part of the compound 'stepbrother', the primary stress shifts to the prefix 'STEP', and 'brother' receives reduced stress. This pattern applies to many compound family words (grandmother, grandfather, stepsister).

speaking.instruction: Say these two sentences with the correct intonation pattern. The first sentence is a yes/no question (rising intonation). The second sentence is a statement with a compliment (falling intonation).
speaking.audioPrompt: Let us practise intonation. First, say this question with rising intonation — your voice goes UP at the end: 'Is that your sister?' Now say this compliment with falling intonation — your voice goes DOWN at the end: 'She is really beautiful!' Try both sentences now.
speaking.targetSentence: Is that your sister? She is really beautiful!
speaking.phonetic: /ɪz ðæt jɔːr ˈsɪstər↗ ʃiː ɪz ˈrɪəli ˈbjuːtɪfʊl↘/
speaking.hint: For the question 'Is that your sister?', imagine your voice is climbing stairs — it goes UP at the end. For the compliment 'She is really beautiful!', imagine your voice is going down a slide — it goes DOWN at the end. The rising tone shows you are asking; the falling tone shows you are making a warm statement.
speaking.explanation: This drill contrasts rising intonation (used in yes/no questions like 'Is that your sister?') with falling intonation (used in statements and compliments like 'She is really beautiful!'). Mastering this contrast is essential for natural English conversation about family, especially when asking about and complimenting family members.

questions.question: In the passage, Lucia says: 'My mother's name is Ana.' What does the 's after 'mother' mean?
options: It shows possession — the name belongs to her mother.
questions.answer: It shows possession — the name belongs to her mother.
questions.explanation: When we write 'My mother's name,' the 's shows that the name belongs to her mother. This is the possessive 's. It is different from the contraction 'She's' (She is).

questions.question: Lucia writes: 'His name is Pedro.' Who does 'His' refer to?
questions.explanation: Just before this sentence, Lucia says: 'I have one brother.' Then she says: 'His name is Pedro.' The possessive adjective 'His' refers to the brother she just mentioned.

questions.question: Which sentence correctly uses the possessive 's?
questions.explanation: To show that the name belongs to the grandmother, we add 's after 'grandmother.' The correct form is 'My grandmother's name is Rosa.' Without the apostrophe and s, the sentence is grammatically incorrect.

questions.question: Lucia says: 'This is my bedroom.' Why does she use 'this' and not 'that'?
options: Because the bedroom is near her — she is pointing to something close.
Because the bedroom is far away from her.
questions.answer: Because the bedroom is near her — she is pointing to something close.
questions.explanation: We use 'this' for something singular that is near us. Lucia is standing in or next to her bedroom, so she says 'This is my bedroom.' If it were far away, she would say 'That is my bedroom.'

questions.question: Lucia writes: 'Those are their children — my cousins, Marco and Bianca.' Why does she use 'those' instead of 'this'?
options: Because she is talking about more than one person who are not right next to her.
Because she is talking about only one person who is near her.
Because 'those' is used for singular nouns.
questions.answer: Because she is talking about more than one person who are not right next to her.
questions.explanation: 'Those' is used for plural people or things that are farther away. Marco and Bianca are two people (plural), and they are not standing right next to Lucia. So 'those' is the correct word.

questions.question: Which word correctly completes this sentence? '_______ is my aunt Sofia. She's very friendly.'
questions.explanation: We need a singular demonstrative because we are talking about one person (Aunt Sofia). 'Those' and 'These' are for plural. 'That' is correct for one person who is not right next to the speaker.

questions.question: According to the passage, which adjective describes Lucia's brother Pedro?
questions.explanation: The passage says: 'Pedro is really helpful at home.' The adjective 'helpful' describes Pedro. 'Generous' describes the grandmother Rosa, and 'friendly' describes Aunt Sofia.

questions.question: Read this sentence from the passage: 'She's my mother's mother.' What does this sentence tell us about Rosa?
options: Rosa is Lucia's grandmother on her mother's side.
questions.answer: Rosa is Lucia's grandmother on her mother's side.
questions.explanation: The sentence 'She's my mother's mother' means Rosa is the mother of Lucia's mother. That makes Rosa Lucia's grandmother. Notice the two possessive forms: 'my mother's' (belonging to my mother) and 'mother' (the person who is her mother).

questions.question: Which sentence expresses a future plan?
options: I am going to visit my grandmother tomorrow.
I visit my grandmother every day.
questions.answer: I am going to visit my grandmother tomorrow.
questions.explanation: 'Be going to' expresses a planned future intention.

questions.prompt: Write a short paragraph (at least 5 sentences) about your family. Introduce at least two family members using demonstratives (this, that, these, those). Describe their good qualities and give at least two compliments. Use possessive adjectives and possessive 's.
questions.criteria: The response must contain at least 5 complete sentences forming a coherent paragraph. The student must correctly use at least one demonstrative (this/that/these/those), at least two possessive adjectives (my, his, her, our, their), at least one possessive 's construction, and at least two compliments using positive adjectives. All sentences must have correct capitalization and end punctuation.
